```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 110)
stopifnot(requireNamespace("stringi", quietly = TRUE),
          requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE),
          requireNamespace("knitr", quietly = TRUE))
library(ggplot2)
source_url <- "https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/dsscapstone/dataset/Coursera-SwiftKey.zip"
files <- c(blogs="en_US.blogs.txt", news="en_US.news.txt", twitter="en_US.twitter.txt")
data_dir <- "data"
dir.create(data_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
zip_file <- file.path(data_dir, "Coursera-SwiftKey.zip")
paths <- file.path(data_dir, "final", "en_US", unname(files))

# If you downloaded the ZIP yourself, save it as data/Coursera-SwiftKey.zip.
# The R Markdown downloads it only if the three extracted files are absent.
if (!all(file.exists(paths))) {
  if (!file.exists(zip_file)) {
    old_timeout <- getOption("timeout")
    options(timeout = max(1800, old_timeout))
    download.file(source_url, destfile = zip_file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
  }
  unzip(zip_file, files = file.path("final", "en_US", unname(files)), exdir = data_dir)
}
if (!all(file.exists(paths))) stop("English corpus files not found after extraction. Check the ZIP and the data/final/en_US folder.")

# Stream each file in chunks rather than loading all 550+ MiB into RAM.
# Word segmentation is Unicode-aware; other tokenizer definitions may differ.
set.seed(20261017)
scan_corpus <- function(path, label, batch_size=10000L, sample_rate=0.005) {
  con <- file(path, open = "rb")
  on.exit(close(con))
  n_lines <- 0L
  n_words <- 0
  n_chars <- 0
  max_chars <- 0L
  sample_list <- list()
  sample_n <- 0L
  repeat {
    rows <- readLines(con, n = batch_size, warn = FALSE, skipNul = TRUE,
                      encoding = "UTF-8")
    if (!length(rows)) break
    rows <- iconv(rows, from = "UTF-8", to = "UTF-8", sub = " ")
    word_counts <- stringi::stri_count_words(rows)
    char_counts <- nchar(rows, type = "chars", allowNA = TRUE)
    n_lines <- n_lines + length(rows)
    n_words <- n_words + sum(word_counts, na.rm=TRUE)
    n_chars <- n_chars + sum(char_counts, na.rm=TRUE)
    max_chars <- max(max_chars, char_counts, na.rm=TRUE)
    chosen <- which(runif(length(rows)) < sample_rate)
    if (length(chosen)) {
      sample_n <- sample_n + 1L
      sample_list[[sample_n]] <- rows[chosen]
    }
  }
  list(source=label, file=basename(path),
       size_mib=as.numeric(file.info(path)$size)/1024^2,
       lines=n_lines, words=n_words, chars=n_chars,
       max_chars=max_chars,
       sample=unlist(sample_list, use.names=FALSE))
}
results <- Map(scan_corpus, paths, names(files))
stats <- data.frame(
  Source = tools::toTitleCase(names(files)),
  File = basename(paths),
  `Size (MiB)` = round(vapply(results, `[[`, numeric(1), "size_mib"),1),
  Lines = as.numeric(vapply(results, `[[`, numeric(1), "lines")),
  Words = as.numeric(vapply(results, `[[`, numeric(1), "words")),
  `Words / line` = round(vapply(results, function(x) x$words/x$lines, numeric(1)),1),
  check.names=FALSE
)
samples <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results, function(x) {
  data.frame(Source=tools::toTitleCase(x$source),
             Words=stringi::stri_count_words(x$sample),
             Text=x$sample,
             stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
}))
# Keep punctuation-robust ASCII words for a small illustrative word-frequency plot.
tokens <- stringi::stri_extract_all_regex(tolower(samples$Text), "[a-z]+(?:'[a-z]+)?")
words_sample <- unlist(tokens, use.names=FALSE)
words_sample <- words_sample[nchar(words_sample) > 1]
frequencies <- sort(table(words_sample), decreasing=TRUE)
top_words <- head(frequencies, 12)
```

> **Management takeaway.** The three English-language sources contain substantial training material but differ strongly in writing style. Tweets are short and conversational; blog posts and news items are longer. We will use those differences to design a small, fast next-word prediction tool rather than train a large model prematurely.

## 1. What data was reviewed?

The project uses the Coursera–SwiftKey corpus: US-English **blogs**, **news** and **Twitter** messages. The R code in this document downloads the source ZIP (if needed), extracts all three `.txt` files and **reads them in 10,000-line batches**. It computes the full-file summaries below, while taking a reproducible 0.5% sample for visualization.

```{r summary-table}
shown <- stats
shown$Lines <- format(shown$Lines, big.mark=",", scientific=FALSE, trim=TRUE)
shown$Words <- format(shown$Words, big.mark=",", scientific=FALSE, trim=TRUE)
knitr::kable(shown, align=c("l","l","r","r","r","r"),
             caption="Table 1 · Full-source file statistics, calculated at knit time")
```

Across the three sources, the analysis covers **`r format(sum(stats$Lines), big.mark=",", scientific=FALSE)` lines** and **`r format(sum(stats$Words), big.mark=",", scientific=FALSE)` word tokens**. Results depend slightly on text-decoding and the definition of a word.

## 2. What stands out?

**Message length varies sharply by source.** The typical number of words in a Twitter record is far below the average blog or news record. A next-word model must therefore learn from both short conversations and longer prose.

```{r length-comparison}
ggplot(stats, aes(x=reorder(Source, `Words / line`), y=`Words / line`, fill=Source)) +
  geom_col(width=.6, show.legend=FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label=sprintf("%.1f", `Words / line`)), hjust=-.18,
            fontface="bold", size=4) +
  coord_flip() +
  expand_limits(y=max(stats$`Words / line`)*1.22) +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Blogs"="#168f91","News"="#5475af","Twitter"="#d6a13d")) +
  labs(title="Average word tokens per text record", x=NULL, y="Words per line") +
  theme_minimal(base_size=13) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y=element_blank())
```

A **sampled histogram** shows the distribution, not just the average. Very long texts are excluded *from this plot only* to keep short records readable. The underlying summary table still uses every line.

```{r sample-histogram}
plot_limit <- as.numeric(quantile(samples$Words, .99, na.rm=TRUE))
plot_rows <- samples[is.finite(samples$Words) & samples$Words <= plot_limit, ]
ggplot(plot_rows, aes(x=Words, fill=Source)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=38, color="white", linewidth=.16, show.legend=FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~Source, ncol=1, scales="free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("Blogs"="#168f91","News"="#5475af","Twitter"="#d6a13d")) +
  labs(title="Distribution of words per line in a reproducible 0.5% sample",
       subtitle=paste("Showing the shortest 99% of sampled lines; cap:", round(plot_limit), "words"),
       x="Words per line", y="Number of sample lines") +
  theme_minimal(base_size=11)
```

**Common words dominate.** In text prediction, frequent words such as articles and prepositions matter; discarding them would remove useful context. The chart below uses the sampled messages across all three sources.

```{r word-frequency}
word_plot <- data.frame(Word=names(top_words), Count=as.integer(top_words))
ggplot(word_plot, aes(x=reorder(Word,Count), y=Count)) +
  geom_col(fill="#168f91",width=.72) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title="Most frequent words in the sampled text", x=NULL, y="Sample occurrences") +
  theme_minimal(base_size=12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y=element_blank())
```

## 3. What the prediction algorithm will do

A user types a few words and the system proposes **three likely next words**. Rather than generate unrestricted sentences, we will train a transparent **n-gram frequency model** on a cleaned, balanced sample. It will:

1. Normalize case and spacing; remove inappropriate material and obvious noise while **keeping common words and contractions** where possible.
2. Count one-, two-, three- and four-word sequences in the training data.
3. Match the user's most recent words to the longest available sequence and **back off** to shorter sequences when the full phrase is unseen.
4. Test on held-out lines, using **top-three next-word accuracy**, coverage and response time. We will compare against a simple frequent-word baseline.

## 4. Planned Shiny app and next decision

The prototype will have one text box, a **Predict** button, and three ranked suggestions. The output will show only the suggestions and a short explanation so that anyone can test it without learning data-science terminology. Performance priorities are **speed, accuracy and a lightweight download**.

**Next milestone:** build and benchmark the first 3-gram/4-gram model, then decide whether larger samples improve accuracy enough to justify the memory cost.

<small><strong>Data and scope:</strong> Coursera–SwiftKey English corpora, <a href="https://d396qusza40orc.cloudfront.net/dsscapstone/dataset/Coursera-SwiftKey.zip">official download</a>. R script calculates all reported metrics from the downloaded files when knitted; samples are reproducible with seed 20261017. The corpus reflects historical online writing, not a representative sample of all English or current usage.</small>
